concept.name: Negative volume index
concept.definition: Paul Dysart's cumulative index (1930s; popularized by Norman Fosback in Stock Market Logic) that accumulates percentage price changes only on periods when volume declines, on the theory that informed 'smart money' acts on quiet days while the crowd trades on high-volume days.
concept.intuition: Strip out the noisy high-volume days and watch what remains: if price grinds higher on falling-volume days, quiet accumulation is presumed.
concept.mechanics: Fosback's version (used by StockCharts): start the index at 1000; when volume falls versus the prior period, apply the period's percentage price change to the index; when volume rises, leave it unchanged. Signals come from NVI relative to its 255-day EMA - above it favors a bull market, below it a bear market.
concept.formula: If V_t < V_{t-1}: NVI_t = NVI_{t-1} x (1 + (C_t - C_{t-1})/C_{t-1}); else NVI_t = NVI_{t-1}. Dysart's original accumulated net market advances instead of percentage price change.
concept.failure_modes: Designed for broad market indexes with exchange volume, it behaves erratically on individual stocks; the 255-day EMA signal lags heavily and whipsaws in volatile stretches.
concept.misconceptions: Fosback's 96%/53% bull/bear odds were results from a 1941-1975 study, not stable laws; and falling volume is not inherently bullish in every market regime.
concept.example: From NVI 1000: volume falls and price rises 0.8%, so NVI = 1008; next day volume rises and price rises 1%, and NVI stays 1008.
